Lessons.Title: More Factors, More Problems
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: solve multiplication stories when the missing number can be the total, the number of equal groups or the size of each group. Use an equation with a symbol where asked, interpret its meaning, and explain a diagram or other strategy. This Edulytics text aligns to first-edition (2021) Grade 3 Unit 1 Lesson 15; it is not a copy of publisher figures or gated material.

Number Talk — Tens (10 minutes): mentally evaluate 1 × 10, 2 × 10, 3 × 10 and 4 × 10, giving 10, 20, 30 and 40. After each, explain why the product increases by ten as the number of groups increases by one. Oral comparison and strategy explanations require a teacher.

Activity 1 — Represent Situations with Equations (15 minutes): original first-edition Student Facing asks for TWO parts in each of three food contexts: an equation with a symbol for the unknown, then the solved number with reasoning. Fifteen plates are five per table: □ × 5 = 15, so 3 tables. Six sandwiches take two slices each: 6 × 2 = □, so 12 slices. Sixty ice cubes in trays of ten: □ × 10 = 60, so 6 trays. The Edulytics source companion presents separate symbolic and numeric fields; a number alone does not satisfy the equation-writing requirement.

Activity 2 — Multiplication Mashup (20 minutes): five distinct source problems. (1) Sixteen socks in piles of two makes 8 piles; (2) eight piles of two makes 16 socks; (3) sixteen socks spread equally among eight piles gives 2 socks in each; (4) nine boxes of five shirts give 45 shirts; (5) eighty sweaters at eight per pile make 10 piles. The first three deliberately distinguish unknown group count, unknown total and unknown group size, while maintaining the related numbers 16, 8 and 2. Students can draw equal groups, tape diagrams or write equations and explain why the chosen model fits. Numeric checks do not replace their oral or drawn explanations.

Synthesis (10 minutes): compare student reasoning and identify which quantity is missing in each situation. A multiplication model describes equal groups; repeated addition can be a strategy for finding a total but is not by itself the definition of multiplication. Preserve the distinction between missing groups, missing objects per group and missing overall total. An original first-party Cool-down can revisit unknown groups with a new situation and teacher-reviewed reasoning; the original first-edition two-part Cool-down text has now been identified in a published 2021 K5_v1 teacher-guide copy; Edulytics paraphrases both source mathematics tasks separately from its independent Cool-down, without copying publisher artwork.

Student section summary: the original first-edition lesson includes an eight-pile-of-two socks representation, followed by expression 8 × 2 and equation 8 × 2 = 16. Explain that a complete equality states a total and distinguishes an expression from an equation. Source image artwork is not embedded.

Accessibility and language support from the 2021 teacher guidance: Engagement in Activity 1 divides each equation-and-solution story into smaller manageable parts with check-ins; MLR8 Discussion Supports in Activity 2 checks unfamiliar words before discussing the five different unknown quantities. Teacher monitors each pair's interpretation and accepts multiple justified representations.

First-edition Student Section Summary makes a visual-to-symbol bridge for Diego's 8 piles of 2 socks: independent eight-compartment tape with each part 2, 8 × 2 as an expression and 8 × 2 = 16 as the solved equation. The first-party Grade 3 companion now shows a separate accessible eight-compartment model; it does not reuse the publisher's original figures. The original first-edition 2021 publisher SVGs and all five pages of the Student Task Statements PDF have now been examined for their mathematical structure. The independent Edulytics drawings give the same eight-by-two grouping without reproducing the source artwork.

The source suggests optional teacher-led Centers: Capture Squares Stage 5 (multiply with 2, 5 and 10), and Five in a Row Stage 8 (addition/subtraction within 1,000 with composing). These are separately supervised game centers, not substitutes for the source lesson or automatically graded online tasks. A teacher reflection focuses on whether all small-group learners' ideas were heard, valued, and accepted.

Source original Cool-down: the 2021 first-edition K5_v1 printed teacher guide identifies TWO tasks in the same five-minute source assessment, one with four boxes holding ten toys each, and another distributing ten socks in piles of two. The teacher reviews each student's reasoning and the different unknown roles. Learner source-subtask prompts are independently paraphrased and should not reveal the expected numerical answers before submission. The independent Edulytics Cool-down on 24 socks is NOT one of these two original source tasks.

Teacher reflection: invite students to distinguish known products, unknown numbers of groups and unknown numbers in a group. Defer general mastery of less familiar facts until a future unit; all student grouping drawings and classroom discussion require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Three unknown roles
KeyConcepts.Definition: In an equal-group story, an unknown may be the number of groups, objects in each group or the total.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Locate which quantity is missing before writing the equation.
KeyConcepts.Example: □ × 5 = 15 asks how many tables; 6 × 2 = □ asks how many bread slices.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equation with unknown symbol
KeyConcepts.Definition: A multiplication equation can include a box or question mark where the value is not yet known.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Where source Activity 1 requires an equation, write the symbol as well as the separate solved numeric answer.

KeyConcepts.Title: Related group facts
KeyConcepts.Definition: Several multiplication stories may use the same factors and product but ask for different quantities.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use 8 × 2 = 16 to reason about eight piles, two socks per pile and sixteen total socks.
KeyConcepts.Example: 16 socks in 8 groups gives 2 socks per group.

KeyConcepts.Title: Expression versus equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: An expression calculates or represents a quantity; an equation asserts equality.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Write 8 × 2 as an expression and 8 × 2 = 16 as an equation.
KeyConcepts.Example: The equal-groups diagram supports either when the task requests it.

KeyConcepts.Title: Section Summary: drawings, tape, expression and equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Represent the same eight piles of two socks as groups, as eight tape partitions, as 8 × 2, and as 8 × 2 = 16.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The tape must contain eight equal groups each labeled two and total sixteen; distinguish the numerical expression from the complete equality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Number Talk: groups of ten
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 1 × 10 through 4 × 10 and describe the change.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count groups of ten, then compare consecutive expressions.
Steps: Four groups give 40; each extra group increases the product by ten.
WorkedExamples.Check: Explanation of the regularity requires teacher judgment.

WorkedExamples.Title: Unknown number of tables
WorkedExamples.Question: Fifteen plates, with five on each table: how many tables?
WorkedExamples.Method: Treat the number of tables, not the number of plates on each table, as the unknown factor.
Steps: Count 5, 10, 15 to find three equal tables.
WorkedExamples.Check: The symbol and numerical answer are separate source requirements.

WorkedExamples.Title: Unknown total bread slices
WorkedExamples.Question: Six sandwiches each use two bread slices. Find the number of slices.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use known groups and group size, leaving the product missing.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the student's grouping drawing or explanation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Unknown number of trays
WorkedExamples.Question: Sixty ice cubes are arranged ten per tray. How many trays?
WorkedExamples.Method: The group size is ten; the number of groups is missing.
Steps: Count by tens to get six trays.
WorkedExamples.Check: The factor meaning matches the context.

WorkedExamples.Title: Three linked sock stories
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain the different unknown roles in the 16-sock and 8-pile contexts.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use a common 8 × 2 = 16 relationship with three different missing positions.
Steps: With 16 socks and 2 per pile, the missing group count is 8.
With 8 piles and 2 socks per pile, the missing total is 16.
With 16 socks in 8 piles, the missing size per pile is 2.
WorkedExamples.Check: The source deliberately tests three distinct unknown roles; teacher assesses why each answer corresponds to the question.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Answering Activity 1 with only a number.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source requires a symbolic equation as a separate product.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Show the multiplication equality containing the unknown symbol, then the solved result.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating 16 socks in 8 piles as 8 socks in each pile.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Eight is the number of groups, not the group size.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Verify 8 equal groups of 2 socks total 16.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming every multiplication story asks for a product.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source includes missing group count and missing group size.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify the unknown role before choosing a strategy.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming a teacher-reviewed drawing or gallery walk was machine-passed.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A numeric checker cannot verify group diagrams, oral discussion or strategy interpretation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record numeric checks separately and require teacher judgment for models and conversation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating the three source missing-number cases as division lessons before division has been introduced.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The first-edition 2021 teacher preparation explicitly defers relating unknown-factor problems to division until a future unit.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use known equal-group facts, skip-counting, tape diagrams and multiplication equations; teacher reviews reasoning.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating the 2021 two-part source Cool-down and Edulytics's one-question skill review as the same assessment.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original first-edition 2021 teacher guide provides two distinct situations; the separately written Edulytics question is supplemental.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep both verified source mathematics tasks as separately labeled, teacher-reasoned source subtasks, and present the additional Edulytics item independently.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up: four tens products (10, 20, 30, 40) and teacher-checked Number Talk reasoning.
Activity 1: three meal-story prompts, each requiring a symbolic equation plus a solved answer and explanation.
Activity 2: five stories with correct numeric outcomes 8, 16, 2, 45 and 10, covering different unknown roles.
Preserve model choices: equal-group drawing, tape diagram, multiplication equation, or explained skip-counting.
Synthesis: identify group count, group size and total, and explain why a method works.
Section summary: source's eight piles of two support expression 8 × 2 and full equation 8 × 2 = 16.

The two first-edition publisher Cool-down mathematics situations were source-text verified from the 2021 K5_v1 guide; the original source image pixels and separate Student Task PDF are still not visually verified. All authored tests are unrun.
